# Introduction {#sec-intro}

<!-- RAP options for this intro (three audiences; RAP 2, tax rates, chosen 2026-09-24): Thesis/feedback/jmp-intro-rap-options.md -->

Sales and value-added taxes that credit purchases reward firms for overreporting their inputs: every fictitious dollar of deductible inputs lowers the tax a firm owes, and the reward grows with the tax rate. Firms act on this incentive. Tax authorities around the world document input overreporting, often through invoices for purchases that never took place [@OECD2017], and the losses they have measured are large: between 1.2% and 2.7% of total tax revenue in Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Poland and Slovakia, and about a ninth of the entire VAT compliance gap in Colombia and Slovakia [@OECD2017; @Carrillo2022; @CASE2018; @Pelaez2022]. Because these figures count only what enforcement detects, true losses are plausibly larger. The gains also accrue at the top: in Ecuador, the tax evaded by inflating costs, as a share of owners' income, is 56 times higher for owners in the top 5% of the income distribution than for those in the bottom 80% [@Carrillo2022].

How individuals' reported income responds to tax rates is well documented; how firms' overreporting of inputs responds is not. For individuals, a large literature estimates how reported income responds to the tax rate and shows that the response includes evasion and avoidance as well as changes in real activity [@Saez2012; @Chetty2009]. For firms, evidence on responses to tax rates comes mostly from bunching at kinks and notches in the tax schedule [@Best2015] and from misreported imports [@FismanWei2004]. Moreover, economic theory suggests that optimal commodity-tax rates should be lower on goods whose evasion is more elastic with respect to the tax rate [@Cremer1993]. Yet, to my knowledge, no study has estimated how firms' overreporting of inputs, a form of tax evasion that the credit on purchases in sales and value-added taxes incentivizes, responds to the tax rate. One reason is that overreporting is not observed in the data: for a given level of output, a firm reporting high input use may be overreporting, or it may suffer from low productivity.

I investigate whether input overreporting rises with the tax rate, and the extent to which it affects government tax revenue through firms' claimed deductions. I find that, after Colombia raised its sales-tax rate in 1983 for most manufacturing industries, while exempt industries remained exempt, overreporting by unincorporated firms increased significantly, reaching about 9% of true materials by 1987 in the industries affected by the tax increase. In a structural model estimated on all industries, I find that a 0.5% increase in the sales-tax rate raises claimed deductions by 16% to 28%, far more than the 0.5% that a naive proportional calculation would suggest, while cuts lower claimed deductions only gradually: the smallest cut distinguishable from current policy is 8%. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that undetected overreporting costs about 3% of potential net sales-tax revenue from unincorporated firms in the sample. Near the current rate, and holding the tax collected on sales fixed, the elasticity of this revenue with respect to the tax rate is about −20: a 1% increase in the rate lowers it by about 20% (@sec-app-backofenvelope).

To distinguish between evasion and productivity, I employ a structural production-function approach, and then use it to study how evasion responds to the tax rate. In the absence of evasion, the first-order condition for materials, the flexible deductible input, reveals the structural relationship between the firm's materials share of revenue and the common technology within the industry. Corporations are closely monitored by the government and face the market's reaction to tax aggressiveness, which keeps them from overreporting; their reports allow me to identify that technology in each industry. Among unincorporated firms, deviations from the common technology reveal overreporting up to measurement error in output. Deconvolution then separates the distribution of overreporting from that of the measurement error, and the production-function estimates recover productivity net of overreporting. To study how overreporting responds to the tax rate, I exploit the 1983 reform, measuring overreporting against the output elasticity of materials identified from corporations. Finally, employing an entropy-based method that does not require specifying the distribution of the unobservables [@Schennach2014], I estimate a structural model in which firms weigh the tax saved on overreported inputs against the probability of detection and a cost of evasion that varies with productivity.

Separating overreporting from productivity also yields three findings of its own. First, a simple test compares unincorporated firms' materials shares with the corporate benchmark in each industry. It rejects the absence of overreporting in 9 of 20 manufacturing industries, including four of the five largest, which together produce more than half of manufacturing output, and it rejects decisively, at the 1% level, in five of them, where unincorporated firms overreport 11% to 25% of their true materials on average. The test is robust: it remains valid under any detection probability and cost of evasion that vanish without evasion, and under any common production technology. A rejection is also unambiguous, because no firm gains by underreporting deductible inputs, so it can only point to overreporting. Second, ignoring overreporting distorts the production function and, with it, measured productivity: in those five industries, correcting for overreporting recovers output elasticities of materials consistently lower than uncorrected estimates [@Gandhi2020], and less dispersed and more persistent productivity distributions, with a ratio of the 90th to the 10th percentile about 40% lower on average and a half-life of productivity shocks two to seven times longer. Third, the structural estimates show a cost of evasion that is convex in productivity and lowest near the 86th percentile of productivity, which rationalizes why evasion rises with firm size but drastically drops at the very top [@Carrillo2022].

These results relate to three strands of public economics and to one of productivity measurement. First, I estimate how a particular form of evasion by firms responds to the tax rate, a response the literature on taxes and revenue has mostly seen through individuals' reported income. Traditionally, the elasticity of personal taxable income has combined all different responses to the rate, evasion included, into a single statistic [@Feldstein1999; @SlemrodKopczuk2002; @Saez2012]. However, when part of the cost of evasion is a transfer rather than a resource cost, this elasticity alone no longer measures the efficiency cost of taxation [@Chetty2009]. Measuring that cost requires knowing how evasion itself responds to the rate, separately from real activity. Direct evidence on this response is scarcer, and comes from the gap between households' consumption and reported income [@Gorodnichenko2009] and, for firms, from bunching at kinks in the tax schedule [@Best2015]. I provide such evidence for firms' overreporting of inputs under a sales tax that credits purchases, from both a statutory rate change and a structural model that separates overreporting from productivity. The structural model also provides an element that the theory of optimal commodity taxation under evasion requires: how claimed deductions respond to the rate [@Cremer1993].

Second, I provide measures of firms' cost overreporting without relying on confidential tax records. Most evidence on firm evasion focuses on underreported revenue [@Slemrod2019]. Yet the cost side matters: firms offset enforcement on revenue by raising reported costs [@Carrillo2017; @Asatryan2017], and paper trails make transactions between firms harder to misreport than sales to final consumers [@Pomeranz2015]; therefore, firms that sell to other firms have little room on sales and more on costs. Cost overreporting has mostly been measured directly with transaction-level tax records in Ecuador and Mexico, which reveal the mechanism: firms acquiring fake invoices from ghost firms [@Carrillo2022; @Zumaya2021]. Tax records, however, are confidential, available for few countries, and accessible only to selected researchers. Survey-based measures of firm evasion rely instead on firms' self-reported share of sales declared to the tax authority [@Dabla2019], whose truthfulness cannot be verified. My approach needs only reported inputs and output, and is thus equally applicable to standard firm-level surveys and administrative records.

Third, I extend the validation-sample approach from individuals to firms. This approach infers evasion by comparing an indirect measure of true income between a truth-reporting group and a group that may misreport. For example, the self-employed report less income relative to their food consumption than employees, whose income is reported by their employers [@Pissarides1989]. Another application finds that about 12% of wages and salaries in Estonia go unreported [@Paulus2015]. The same comparison has also been used to measure how evasion responds to a tax reform [@Gorodnichenko2009]. For firms, however, the natural indirect measure, output relative to inputs, also depends on an additional unobservable, productivity: a firm reporting high input use may be overreporting or may simply have had a negative productivity shock. I use the production function to separate the two, with corporations as the truth-reporting group. Unlike the comparisons for individuals, mine does not require the two groups to be alike in size or productivity: corporations are much larger than unincorporated firms, and the production function accounts for the differences in productivity behind this gap.

Finally, [the paper]{.content-visible when-meta="jmp"}[this thesis]{.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"} shows how tax-motivated misreporting of inputs distorts production-function estimates. Proxy-variable methods rely on a flexible input, typically materials, either inverting its demand [@Levinsohn2003; @Ackerberg2015] or using its first-order condition [@Gandhi2020], and treat reported inputs as true. Work on mismeasured inputs has focused on classical, mean-zero measurement error, mostly in capital [@Collard2020]. Overreporting differs on both counts: it is an optimal choice that varies with productivity, so it is neither mean zero nor independent of productivity, and it affects exactly the input on which these methods rely. Correcting for it reveals that the output elasticity of materials is consistently lower than uncorrected estimates and that productivity distributions are less dispersed and more persistent, findings that matter for any analysis built on measured productivity differences across firms.

The rest of the paper follows the argument. @sec-model shows why a firm would overreport materials and what holds it back, and @sec-setting explains why Colombian corporations can serve as truth-tellers. @sec-testing shows that overreporting can be detected and measured from production data alone, and @sec-pf what correcting for it does to production-function estimates. @sec-fiscal uses the 1983 reform to show that overreporting responds to the tax rate, and @sec-counterfactual asks how much claimed deductions would move under other rates. @sec-conclusion, as tradition demands, concludes.
:::
